descriptions.text: ~$2M taken from Revest Finance. “One audit is never enough” says Revest, as they found that a reentrancy vulnerability was not picked up in their security checks.

classic re-entrancy pattern: use fnftId -> external call with callback mechanism -> update fnftId. Vulnerable code snippet: Attack tx: https://etherscan.io/tx/0xe0b0c2672b760bef4e2851e91c69c8c0ad135c6987bbf1f43f5846d89e691428 Analysis: https://blocksecteam.medium.com/revest-finance-vulnerabilities-more-than-re-entrancy-1609957b742f

DeFi protocol Revest Finance has been hacked. Hackers stole nearly 7.7 million ECO, 579 LYXe, nearly 715 million BLOCKS, and over 350,000 RENA. According to SlowMist analysis, this attack is because the handleMultipleDeposits function in the tokenVault contract does not determine whether the newly minted NFT exists, so the attacker uses this point to directly modify the information of the NFT that has been minted, and in the Revest contract The key functions in this are not restricted by reentrant locks, which lead to being used by callbacks.

On March 27, 2022, Revest Finance was exploited via a reentrancy vulnerability affecting its Ethereum smart contracts, resulting in losses exceeding $2 million across several supported tokens. The attacker manipulated the FNFT minting flow to mint and redeem tokens without backing deposits, draining vaults for assets including RENA, BLOCKS, ECO, LYXe, and others. The root cause was a reentrancy vulnerability in the FNFT minting and deposit mechanism. Specifically, the protocol failed to update internal accounting variables before allowing external calls, permitting reentrant manipulation of FNFT supply and vault balances to mint and redeem unbacked tokens.

The Revest protocol was targeted with an attack that stole $BLOCKS, $ECO, and $RENA tokens from their vault. The protocol wrote that the attacker used a "highly sophisticated attack on a vulnerability that went unnoticed during our Solidity.Finance audit as well as ... multiple peer-reviews". The hacker quickly swapped the stolen tokens for ETH via various decentralized exchanges, then tumbled the funds using Tornado Cash. The protocol wrote that they "do not possess the funds needed for meaningful financial recompense, and are not covered by any DeFi insurance provider", but promised to try to "do everything within our power to make things as right as they can possibly be made".
